books.title: The Richest Man in Babylon
books.author: George S. Clason
books.description: Timeless money lessons told as parables set in ancient Babylon.
ideas: Pay yourself first

In George Clason's parables, the richest man in ancient Babylon reveals his secret: a part of everything you earn is yours to keep. Before you pay the baker, the landlord or the merchant, pay your future self, at least a tenth. It sounds obvious, but most people do the opposite: they spend first and save whatever is left, and usually nothing is left. Treating savings like a bill you owe yourself flips the order. Today: set up an automatic transfer of a fixed slice of your next pay, even 5 or 10 percent, into a separate account you don't touch.
pay-yourself-first
Make your gold work

Saving money is only the first step, Clason's Arkad explains. Each coin you keep should become a worker that brings in more coins, and those coins should work too, until you have an army of them. In modern terms, that means putting savings into investments that grow over time instead of leaving them idle. Money sitting in a drawer loses value to inflation; money invested patiently can multiply. Today: look at where your savings currently sit, and learn about one simple, low-cost way to let them grow, such as a broad index fund.
Control your expenses

What we call necessary expenses, Clason warned, always grow to match our income unless we push back. Earn more and we find new necessities: a bigger flat, a nicer car, more takeaways. That's why some people on high salaries are always broke. The answer isn't misery but intention: decide what you truly value and budget for it, rather than letting spending happen by default. Today: look at last month's spending and find one "necessary" expense that's really a habit. Decide whether it still earns its place.
Guard against loss

In one parable, a man loses his savings by lending them to a brickmaker who promises to buy rare jewels. The lesson is that before chasing high returns, protect what you already have. Seek advice from people who actually know the field, not from enthusiastic friends or salespeople, and be wary of schemes that promise quick riches. A small, safe return is better than a big loss. Today: before your next investment or loan, ask yourself who is advising you, what they know, and what you'd lose if it went wrong.
Increase your ability to earn

Clason's characters also stress that wealth grows faster when your earning power grows. The more you learn, the more skilfully you work, and the more you're trusted, the more you can earn. Skills, unlike money, can't be stolen or lost in a bad deal. Investing in yourself, through courses, books, mentors and practice, is one of the most reliable investments there is. Today: pick one skill that would make you more valuable at work and spend thirty minutes learning it this week.

books.title: The Psychology of Money
books.author: Morgan Housel
books.description: Short stories about how people actually think about money, and why behaviour matters more than knowledge.
ideas: Compounding needs time, not genius

Warren Buffett is one of the richest people alive, but most of his fortune came after his sixties, because he started investing as a child and never stopped. Morgan Housel uses this to make a point that sounds boring but is powerful: long-term wealth comes less from brilliant returns than from decent returns sustained for a very long time. The secret ingredient is time, and time only works if you avoid ruin and stay invested through bad years. Today: if you're not investing yet, start with a small amount, and make your main goal to never stop.
compounding-time
Wealth is what you don't see

When you see someone driving a £100,000 car, the only thing you know for sure is that they have £100,000 less than before, or a large loan. Housel points out that wealth is mostly invisible: it's the car not bought, the money left in the account, the options kept open. Spending to look rich is one of the fastest ways to have less money. Real wealth is quiet. Today: think about one purchase you were considering mostly to impress other people, and imagine the freedom that money could buy you instead.
Enough

The hardest financial skill, Housel says, is getting the goalpost to stop moving. If your expectations rise every time your income does, no amount will ever feel like enough, and you may risk what you have chasing what you don't need. Several talented people have gone to prison or gone broke because they wanted more when they already had plenty. Knowing what "enough" looks like for you is a form of freedom. Today: write down what "enough" would actually mean for you: income, savings, the life you want. Having a number helps you recognise when you've reached it.
Room for error

Plans almost always meet surprises: a job loss, a sick parent, a market crash. Housel argues that the most important part of any financial plan is room for error. A cash buffer, modest assumptions and not borrowing to the limit let you survive bad luck long enough for good luck to arrive. People who plan for everything going right are often the ones wiped out when it doesn't. Today: if you don't have one, start an emergency fund, even a small one, and treat it as untouchable.
Freedom is the highest dividend

Housel believes the highest dividend money pays is control over your time: the ability to do what you want, when you want, with whom you want. Studies on happiness find that a sense of control over one's life predicts wellbeing better than income itself. Savings give you choices: to leave a bad job, take a risk or spend a month with a newborn. That freedom is worth more than most things money can buy. Today: think about one decision you'd make differently if you had six months of expenses saved. Let that picture motivate your next saving step.
Reasonable beats rational

On paper, the perfectly rational investment strategy might be very aggressive. In real life, it's useless if it scares you into selling everything at the worst moment. Housel suggests aiming to be reasonable rather than coldly rational: choose a plan you can actually stick with when markets fall and the news is frightening. A good strategy you follow beats a perfect one you abandon. Today: ask yourself honestly how you'd feel if your investments fell by a third tomorrow. If the answer is panic, your plan may be too risky for you.

books.title: Rich Dad Poor Dad
books.author: Robert T. Kiyosaki
books.description: A contrast between two father figures and their beliefs about money, work and assets.
ideas: Assets versus liabilities

Robert Kiyosaki offers a simple definition that changes how many people see their finances: an asset puts money in your pocket, and a liability takes money out. By that test, a rental flat that earns more than it costs is an asset, while a big house with a large mortgage and high bills may mostly be a liability, even if it feels like an investment. The goal is to gradually acquire things that pay you rather than things you pay for. Today: list what you own and mark each item as money in or money out. The result may surprise you.
The rat race

Kiyosaki describes a cycle many people live in: earn more, spend more, take on bigger bills, so you need to earn even more. He calls it the rat race: running hard on a wheel that never gets you anywhere. Escaping it means building some income that doesn't depend on trading each hour for pay, from investments, a small business or something you created once that keeps earning. Today: brainstorm three small ways you could earn money that isn't tied directly to your hours, and pick one to explore this month.
Financial literacy

Schools teach us how to work for money, Kiyosaki complains, but rarely how money works. Many people with good salaries still struggle because they never learned to read a budget, understand debt or think about cash flow. Financial literacy isn't about becoming an accountant; it's about understanding the basics well enough to make good decisions and not be fooled. A few books and some honest bookkeeping can change a life. Today: track every expense for one week and add up where your money really goes.
Ask how you can afford it

Saying "I can't afford it" closes the conversation, Kiyosaki notes. Asking "How could I afford it?" opens one. The second question forces your brain to look for solutions: a side income, a cheaper alternative, a plan to save over time. It doesn't mean buying everything you want; it means not letting your current situation become a permanent limit on your thinking. Today: take something you've said you can't afford, a course or a trip, and spend ten minutes brainstorming realistic ways you might make it possible.

books.title: Your Money or Your Life
books.author: Vicki Robin & Joe Dominguez
books.description: A nine-step programme for transforming your relationship with money and reaching financial independence.
ideas: Money is life energy

Every time you buy something, you're paying with hours of your life, the hours you spent earning that money. Vicki Robin and Joe Dominguez suggest calculating your real hourly wage: take your pay, subtract commuting, work clothes and the takeaways you buy because you're exhausted, and divide by all the hours work really takes, including the commute. Suddenly that £60 jacket might cost five hours of your life. Today: work out your real hourly wage, then look at your next planned purchase and ask whether it's worth that many hours.
Track every cent

For one month, the authors suggest, record every single penny that comes in and goes out, every coffee and every parking fee. No budget, no rules, just honest tracking. Many people find that awareness alone changes their spending, because it's hard to keep buying things you've had to write down. You also discover where money quietly leaks away. It's not about guilt but about seeing clearly. Today: start a simple note on your phone and log every expense for the next seven days.
Fulfilment curve

Spending makes us happier up to a point. Money for survival makes a huge difference, comforts a big one, a few luxuries a pleasant one. Beyond that, the authors argue, more stuff brings clutter, worry and maintenance rather than joy. They call the peak of this curve "enough". Knowing where your enough lies lets you stop chasing more and redirect money to what truly matters: freedom, relationships and experiences. Today: walk through your home and notice three things you bought that added little to your happiness. What does that tell you about your enough?
The crossover point

Financial independence, in this book's terms, arrives at the crossover point: the moment when your monthly investment income is greater than your monthly expenses. From then on, work becomes optional. The surprising insight is that lowering your spending gets you there faster than earning more, because it shrinks the target and increases your savings at the same time. Today: calculate how much your monthly expenses are, and estimate how much you'd need invested to cover them. Even if the number seems far away, knowing it makes the path visible.

books.title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
books.author: John C. Bogle
books.description: The founder of Vanguard makes the case for low-cost index funds.
ideas: Own the whole market

Searching for the one brilliant stock is like hunting for a needle in a haystack. John Bogle, founder of Vanguard, had a simpler idea: buy the whole haystack. A broad index fund owns a small piece of every company in a market, so you get the market's overall return at very low cost, without needing to pick winners. It's boring, and that's the point. Over decades, this simple approach has beaten most professionals. Today: look up what a broad, low-cost index fund is in your country, and read one page about how it works.
Costs matter enormously

A 1 percent annual fee sounds tiny. But over thirty or forty years, compounding works against you, and that small fee can swallow a large share of what you would have earned. Bogle hammered this point home: in investing, you get what you don't pay for. Every penny paid in fees, commissions and trading costs is a penny that doesn't grow for you. Choosing low-cost funds is one of the few investment decisions entirely within your control. Today: check the fees on any investments or pension you have. If you don't know them, find out.
Most active funds lose

Most actively managed funds, run by professionals trying to beat the market, fail to do so over long periods once their fees are counted. Some succeed for a few years, but it's almost impossible to predict which ones will keep succeeding. Bogle saw this as a strong argument for index funds: instead of betting on finding the rare winner, simply own the market and keep costs low. Today: if you're paying a manager to pick investments for you, look at how their results compare with a simple index over ten years.
Don't just do something, stand there

When markets fall, the instinct is to act: sell, switch funds, chase the latest trend. Bogle's advice was the opposite: don't just do something, stand there. Frequent trading adds costs and mistakes, and investors who jump in and out often end up buying high and selling low. The most effective strategy for most people is to buy sensible investments, keep adding regularly and leave them alone for a very long time. Today: if you invest, consider checking your account less often. A calm investor is usually a richer one.

books.title: I Will Teach You to Be Rich
books.author: Ramit Sethi
books.description: A practical six-week programme for automating your finances and spending guilt-free on what you love.
ideas: Automate your money

Willpower is a terrible financial plan. Ramit Sethi suggests making good decisions automatic. On payday, set up transfers that move money to savings, investments and bills before you ever see it in your spending account. You can't spend what isn't there, and you don't have to fight yourself every month. Once the system runs, it quietly builds wealth while you get on with life. Today: set up one automatic transfer for the day after your next payday, even a small one, so saving happens without you.
Spend extravagantly on what you love

Sethi's version of frugality isn't about giving up all small pleasures. It's about spending extravagantly on the things you love and cutting mercilessly on the things you don't. If travel lights you up, spend on travel and skip the expensive gym you never use. If you love good food, enjoy it and drive an older car. The aim is a life that feels rich to you, not one that looks rich to others. Today: name your two money joys, the things you'd happily spend more on, and two expenses you wouldn't miss.
Conscious spending plan

Instead of a complicated budget, Sethi proposes a conscious spending plan with four buckets: fixed costs like rent and bills, investments, savings goals such as a holiday or a deposit, and guilt-free spending on anything you like. If your fixed costs are reasonable and the first three buckets are funded automatically, you can spend the rest without guilt. It's simple enough to actually stick to. Today: roughly sort your monthly income into these four buckets and see whether the proportions feel right to you.
Focus on big wins

People agonise over skipping a £3 coffee while ignoring decisions worth thousands: negotiating a salary, refinancing a loan, choosing a cheaper home. Sethi calls these big wins. A single successful salary negotiation can be worth more than a lifetime of skipped lattes. Focus your energy on the few decisions that really move the needle, and relax about the small stuff. Today: identify one big-ticket area, such as your pay, rent, insurance or bank fees, and spend an hour researching how to improve it.

books.title: The Almanack of Naval Ravikant
books.author: Eric Jorgenson
books.description: Naval Ravikant's ideas on building wealth and finding happiness, collected from his tweets, podcasts and essays.

free.note: Free PDF and EPUB from the official site. Not licensed for redistribution, so download it there.

ideas: Seek wealth, not money or status

Naval Ravikant separates three things people chase. Money is how we move time and value between people. Status is our rank in a social hierarchy, and it's zero-sum: someone has to be lower for you to be higher. Wealth is assets that earn while you sleep, like businesses, investments, code or creative work that keeps paying off. Chasing status creates conflict; building wealth can lift everyone. Today: ask yourself whether your current ambitions are really about wealth and freedom, or about status and comparison.
Specific knowledge

The skills that make you hard to replace usually can't be taught in a classroom, Naval argues. He calls this specific knowledge: the unusual mix of interests and talents that feels like play to you and looks like work to others. It's often found by following your genuine curiosity rather than what's fashionable. Someone who loves both biology and storytelling might become a brilliant science writer. Today: list three things you could talk about for hours without getting bored, and ask how they might combine into something valuable.
Leverage multiplies judgment

In the past, multiplying your impact required permission: other people's labour or capital. Today there's a new kind of leverage that doesn't: code and media. A program or a video can serve millions of people at almost no extra cost. Naval's point is that combining good judgment with this kind of leverage can create huge value. One person with a laptop can build something that reaches the world. Today: think of one thing you know or do well, and imagine how a piece of writing, a video or a simple tool could share it with far more people.
Play long-term games with long-term people

The biggest returns in life, Naval says, come from compound interest, and not just in money. Relationships, skills and reputation compound too. Someone you've worked with honestly for ten years trusts you in ways a stranger never will. That's why he advises playing long-term games with long-term people: choose partners, friends and projects you'd happily stick with for decades, and keep showing up. Today: think of one relationship worth investing in for the long run, and do something small to strengthen it.
Happiness is a skill

Naval treats happiness less as something you find and more as a skill you can practise, like fitness. He suggests habits that train it: meditating, exercising, spending time in nature, reducing unnecessary desires and being grateful. He also notes that a desire is a little contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get what you want, so choosing desires carefully matters. Today: pick one craving that's been nagging you, and ask whether it's worth the discomfort of wanting it. Letting go of it might be the quicker route to feeling good.
